prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place GLP-1 first, and I do not take that as evidence of merit by itself. The merit is that this is an unusually complete chain from basic hormone physiology to a medicine. Proglucagon processing, the incretin effect and the identity and action of the truncated active peptide led to receptor biology and then to protracted-action agonists. These drugs now change outcomes in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease. The work has been confirmed independently and at very large scale, so there is no question of prematurity. A prize that spans physiology and its translation is consistent with the physiology-or-medicine mandate. My trio of Holst, Drucker and Knudsen covers the physiology of the active hormone, the receptor and tissue biology, and the molecular design that made a durable therapy possible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited names compete for three places, and the peptide-identification priority (Mojsov, and Habener outside the supplied credit) is contested in a way I cannot resolve from the file. Any trio will look unfair to someone. A second reservation is that including an industrial drug designer shifts the prize from discovery toward development. The committee could reasonably prefer a purely discovery-based trio, and it could prefer to wait until the attribution question is clearer. I also accept that if the committee is reluctant to credit drug development, B006 is the cleaner configuration, with a fully mature mechanism, two unambiguous names and no priority fight.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B005, treating Knudsen's industrial drug-development role as real but outside a three-person cap, and notes that the Mojsov credit is contested.
responses.response: I take the discovery-first logic seriously, and it gives a coherent set. I still prefer Knudsen to Mojsov. The medical significance of GLP-1 rests on a stable, long-acting molecule, and the acylation-based design that made liraglutide and semaglutide possible is an original contribution, not a routine optimisation. Mojsov's contribution is credited in the file, but you yourself flag it as contested, and I cannot adjudicate it. I would not drop the person whose work most directly produced the therapy in favour of a credit I cannot verify. Where we agree is that a discovery-only trio is a legitimate alternative, and that the Mojsov question stays open for me.

responses.point: Ranks BCR-ABL inhibition third, as the paradigm of molecularly targeted therapy with more than twenty years of survival data, but notes that the foundational cytogenetic and fusion-gene discoveries are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree on the clinical impact and maturity of B050. I ranked it lower because of the attribution gap you identify. The prize would honour compound development and clinical proof while the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL fusion work sits outside the credited set, so the narrative would be incomplete. I also think its main contribution is the paradigm, which has since been reproduced many times, while the GLP-1 story combines the paradigm with a distinct biological discovery. If the committee wants a targeted-therapy prize I would consider it, but the credited names give it a weaker claim than B006 or B021 in my view.

responses.point: Ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as the unbroken line from hormone physiology to drug design, but asks whether a basic-plus-drug-design configuration is preferable to a purely physiological one.
responses.response: We agree on the trio, so I will address your open question directly. Splitting physiology from drug design into separate prize parts would require a second distinct achievement, and with a three-person cap that is not workable without dropping one of them. A single citation that states the chain explicitly is the better design. The argument for combining them is the very unbroken line you describe, because Knudsen's work would not have been possible without the physiology, and the physiology reached patients through it. I do not regard the combined configuration as an indulgence towards industry. I would only qualify that we should not let consensus on this trio hide the fact that the Mojsov question is not resolved.

responses.point: Ranks cGAS-STING fourth with Chen, Barber and Ishikawa, arguing that the mechanism is original and of broad biomedical reach but that therapeutic validation is not yet established.
responses.response: I agree that cGAS-STING is a clear and elegant mechanism, and Chen's role in cGAS and cGAMP is decisive. I would qualify two points. First, therapeutic translation is early, and you accept this, so I think timing argues for waiting. Second, the attribution is harder than the three-name credit suggests, because you note that the first authors of the cGAS work are excluded, and I would want to see how the STING identification is split among several groups before crediting Ishikawa. I would therefore keep it as a later candidate, not this year's, though I think it will become strong.

responses.point: Ranks optogenetics fourth, but questions its fit to the medical mandate because it is a methodological invention with limited medical benefit so far, and flags the six-name allocation problem.
responses.response: I share both of your concerns, and they are the reason I rank B042 below the clinical and mechanistic candidates despite its scientific importance. I do not agree that a tool is disqualified, since the prize has honoured methods when they opened a field, and this one has opened causal circuit physiology. But the combination of six credited names, a three-person cap and still-early clinical use means there is no clean configuration. Choosing Deisseroth, Miesenböck and Hegemann, as I did in my opening, excludes Nagel, Bamberg and Boyden, and I accept that this is a weak compromise. I would not put it in the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the contested Mojsov priority, with Habener outside the supplied credit, should outweigh Knudsen's drug-design role in the third place.
Whether the committee will accept an industry scientist as a laureate when a discovery-only trio is available.
Whether B006 should be preferred as the cleaner and more mature configuration if no consensus on GLP-1 attribution emerges.
For B021, whether the original CAR concept (Eshhar and others, not in the supplied credit) makes any configuration of the three credited names unfair.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. The profile records eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, a fellow committee member, and a spatial-transcriptomics paper (Science 2016). Neither involves a shortlisted candidate, and I infer no personal tie from them.
